In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This important resource paper describes a collection of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) produced from patients with a microdeletion of the 16p11.2 chromosomal locus, well-known to be associated with significant neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric abnormalities. The work provides both a cautionary tale about some unexpected consequences of the reprogramming process, as well as a plethora of information about changes in gene expression observed when neural progenitors are derived from these iPSCs. The results provided here, combined with the availability of these iPSCs from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative, should be useful to developmental neurobiologists, those interested in psychiatric disease, and, frankly, to anyone interested in large-scale iPSC-based disease modeling.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "16p11.2 CNV Imparts Transcriptional Alterations in Neural Development in an hiPSC Model of Corticogenesis" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary:

The authors produced 65 iPSC clones from 13 individuals with CNVs at the 16p11.2 locus – 10 with microdeletions and 3 with microduplications. This locus is well-known to be associated with neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric abnormalities. The donor cells were provided by the Simons Foundation who also will make the iPSC clones available, making this a valuable cellular resource for those interested in this chromosomal locus and its role in brain development and function. The authors carried out a detailed analysis of the iPSC clones, produced using episomal reprogramming vectors, finding that many of the clones were compromised by unexpected, random integration of the reprogramming vectors with consequent effects on gene transcription in derived cells. The production of this large set of iPSC clones, as well as the cautionary tale concerning vector integration and a detailed RNAseq analysis of the integration-free clones make this paper, as a Tools and Resource publication, a valuable resource for the community.

Revisions for this paper:

We are mindful that additional experiments cannot be readily done at the moment. However, we believe that addressing some of these points, together with a reanalysis of the current data, will make this paper more useful to those interested in this area:

1) The data in this paper are restricted to iPSCs generated by episomal reprogramming. Since many, perhaps most, investigators are using Sendai virus, the authors should mention that point. Also do they conclude that episomal reprogramming should be avoided?

2) The analysis uses each clone a separate entity. As best as the reviewers can judge, 6 affected donors, not all of whom were diagnosed with ASD, 3 of which had 3 clones, 1 of which had 2 and the other 2 had 1 each, were used. There were also 3 unaffected donors (with 3, 2, and 2 clones). However, clones should not be weighted the same as individual donors. From Hoffman et al. Nat Comm 2017: "Due to the "repeated measures" study design where individuals are represented by multiple independent hiPSC-NPC and hiPSC-neuron lines, we used a linear mixed model by applying the duplicateCorrelation function in our limma/voom analysis. This approach is widely used to control the false positive rate in studies of repeated measures and its importance in hiPSC data sets was recently emphasized (citing Germain and Testa SCR 2017)". We recommend that the authors reanalyze their data so that each entry is a patient-associated value, rather than a clone-associated one.

3) Based on the results shown in this paper, it is a bit misleading to "strongly suggest" that "16p11.2 deletion may impact many functions important to neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric disease" – given that the transcriptional changes reported are quite limited and that no data of any observable phenotype was presented. It would be appropriate to tone down that statement and draw more conservative conclusions.

4) Unless the authors wish to include data for the duplication clones, The title "16p11.2 CNV imparts…" should be "16p11.2 microdeletion imparts…" since all duplication hiPSC clones in the analysis were excluded in the analysis steps of Figure 5 and 6.

5) QC questions:

a) Information on the controls is lacking in the main manuscript. Could the authors specifically clarify (in the Results or Materials and methods) the extent to which cases and controls are sex-, ethnicity- and age-matched, as well as whether they were reprogrammed together with the cases and by the same methods?

b) What was the polygenic risk score for the patients/controls? Might this have accounted for variable clinical presentations?

c) Were the hiPSCs karyotyped?

d) What QC was performed on RNAseq to confirm sample identity, cell type composition, etc? It would be helpful if the authors applied variance partition to uncover to what extent variation is explained by reprogramming method, genotype, donor, diagnosis, cell type, etc?

e) What is the Spearman's correlation coefficients for transcriptomic gene expression between donors and clones samples?

6) Questions involving additional useful data analysis

a) Integration with existing datasets and psychiatric genetic studies: Is there an enrichment of 16p11.2 DEGs for the GWAS loci for ASD, SZ or ADHD? Can the authors also test for enrichment of postmortem disease signatures as reported by the CommonMind Consortium, NIH HBCC and/or PsychEncode UCLA (Geschwind) analyses?

b) Are gene expression differences validated in existing 16p11.2 postmortem, hiPSC or mouse datasets (ie. PMID: 26829649)?

c) Given some recent discussions of convergence between CNV effects in psychiatric disease, are major findings from 16p11.2 conserved in hiPSC neuron datasets from other major CNVs (ie. 22q11.2 hiPSC PMID: 27846841 and mouse PMID: 29666363; 15q11.2 BioRxiv https://doi.org/10.1101/772541; NRXN1 PMID: 31784728)

d) Can the authors discuss whether they believe the genome-wide transcriptomic effects of 16p11.2 reflect chromatin loops between the CNV locus and other target genes? miR targets? Or downstream impacts of perturbed neuronal maturation/activity/signaling?

7) Are the authors able to comment on any phenotypic differences that they did observe between microdeletion lines and wt lines?

Revisions expected in follow-up work:

1) Characterization of micro-duplication lines.

2) Elaboration of phenotypic differences at the neural progenitor stage or in differentiated neurons.

results.result: 16p11.2 CNVs are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and reciprocal physiological phenotypes. The 16p11.2 region spans 29.4-32.2 Mb and encompasses 29 genes. Deletions and duplications at this locus are found in approximately 1% of ASD individuals and 0.01-0.1% of the general population, with reciprocal effects on head size, brain volume, and body mass index.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C22 establish the known associations between 16p11.2 CNVs and various phenotypes based on extensive prior literature. All claims are supported by multiple citations to published research and represent well-established knowledge in the field. These background claims provide appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: A cohort of 65 hiPSC clones was generated from 13 individuals with 16p11.2 CNVs. The cohort includes 10 deletion donors (7 males, 3 females, ages 6-41 years) and 3 duplication donors (2 females, 1 male, ages 5-38 years), with diverse clinical presentations including articulation disorder, ASD, and language disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C23-C28 describe the study cohort with specific demographic and clinical data. The information is clearly documented and represents primary data collection. The cohort size and diversity are appropriate for the study objectives, though the small number of duplication donors (n=3) is noted as a limitation.

results.result: hiPSCs were successfully generated using episomal reprogramming vectors and validated for pluripotency. All clones showed >95% positivity for pluripotency markers, could differentiate into all three germ layers, were confirmed diploid, and had 16p11.2 CNV breakpoints consistent with previously reported values.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 describe standard hiPSC generation and quality control procedures with appropriate validation methods. The immunofluorescence, differentiation assays, and SNP array data provide multiple lines of evidence for successful reprogramming and clone authenticity. The methods are well-established and appropriately applied.

results.result: 40 hiPSC clones were differentiated into cortical neural progenitor cells using dual-SMAD inhibition. Flow cytometry confirmed rapid loss of OCT4 and induction of PAX6 within 7 days. All clones formed neural rosettes with no subjective differences between WT and CNV clones, and showed enrichment for anterior and dorsal cortical markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 describe the neural differentiation protocol and validation. The flow cytometry data (C35), morphological observations (C36), and RNA-seq analysis (C37) provide converging evidence for successful cortical NPC differentiation. The lack of obvious morphological differences at this stage is an important negative result.

results.result: Unexpected integration of episomal reprogramming vectors was detected in many clones, causing major transcriptional artifacts. PCA revealed segregation by integration status rather than genotype. Approximately 40% of OCT3/4 transcripts were plasmid-derived in integration-positive clones, leading to 3,612 differentially expressed genes and significant proliferation changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C47, C109-C111 describe a critical quality control finding. The pseudo-alignment approach (C39-C41) provides quantitative evidence for plasmid expression, and the differential expression analysis (C43-C46) demonstrates the magnitude of the artifact. The conclusion to exclude integration-positive clones (C47) is well-justified. This represents rigorous quality control and methodological innovation.

results.result: A customizable bioinformatic strategy was developed to detect random integration and expression of reprogramming vectors. The authors emphasize the importance of screening for cryptic plasmid integration even when using episomal reprogramming methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C108 describe the methodological contribution. The pseudo-alignment pipeline successfully identified integration events that would have confounded the analysis. This is a valuable methodological advance for the field, though the generalizability depends on the availability of plasmid sequences and appropriate bioinformatic expertise.

results.result: An insufficient number of integration-free 16p11.2 duplication clones remained (n=4) for meaningful analysis, limiting the study to deletion clones only.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 acknowledges a significant limitation of the study. With only 4 integration-free duplication clones, statistical power would be inadequate for robust differential expression analysis. This is an honest assessment of the data limitations.

results.result: After excluding integration-positive clones, DEL and WT populations clustered by genotype. Of 56 genes in the 16p11.2 locus, 14 were differentially expressed and all were downregulated, consistent with copy number-dependent effects. In total, 107 DE genes were identified (49 with ≥1.5-fold change), validated by qPCR for key genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C56 present the core differential expression findings. The PCA clustering (C49), identification of 14 downregulated genes in the deletion interval (C51), and qPCR validation (C55) provide strong evidence. The consistency across individual clones (C56) strengthens confidence in the findings. The statistical approach using DESeq2 with appropriate batch correction is sound.

results.result: Only a subset of 16p11.2 genes are expressed in early NPCs. Of 56 genes in the region, 15 are expressed at or below detection limits, while the remaining 41 are likely relevant to early cortical development. The 14 downregulated genes warrant increased scrutiny as potential drivers of developmental outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C75-C77 provide important context about gene expression in the 16p11.2 region. The identification of which genes are expressed at this developmental stage (C75) is valuable for prioritizing mechanistic studies. The interpretation that expressed genes are likely relevant (C76) is reasonable, though speculative. The recommendation for further study (C77) is appropriate.

results.result: 93 additional DE genes outside the 16p11.2 region were identified, including genes associated with ASD (CNTNAP2, LHFPL3) and excitatory synapse function. These genes impinge on signaling pathways relevant to previously described phenotypic abnormalities in neurons and human carriers.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C72-C73, C83-C84 describe secondary transcriptional effects. The enrichment for ASD-associated genes (C57) is statistically significant, and the identification of synaptic genes (C84) provides mechanistic hypotheses. However, the connection to 'previously described phenotypic abnormalities' (C73) is interpretive and would require functional validation.

results.result: MAPK3 (Erk1) is downregulated and interacts with several other DE genes, supporting a role for the Erk1 MAPK pathway in 16p11.2 phenotypes. However, no changes in NPC proliferation were observed between WT and deletion lines, suggesting MAPK3 may not influence NPC proliferation in these patient lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 present findings about MAPK3. The downregulation is well-documented (C78), and the connection to prior work is appropriate (C79). The negative proliferation result (C80) is important and consistent with prior studies (C82). However, the conclusion that MAPK3 'may not influence' proliferation (C81) is tentative—the lack of effect could reflect compensatory mechanisms or timing issues rather than lack of involvement.

results.result: KCTD13 and TAOK2, both downregulated in deletion lines, have known roles in synaptic transmission and neuronal morphology. Reduced expression in cortical progenitors may impact cortical network development and synaptic tone in autistic individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 cite prior functional studies, but C87 is highly speculative. The connection between reduced expression in NPCs and later synaptic phenotypes requires functional validation. The 'may impact' language (C87) appropriately indicates speculation, but the causal chain from NPC gene expression to mature circuit function is not established.

results.result: The microRNA miR-6723 showed the highest fold-change and smallest p-value among DE transcripts. miR-6723 is enriched in neurons and has been associated with cellular proliferation or immune response in other contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 identify miR-6723 as the most significantly changed transcript. However, the authors acknowledge their sequencing protocol was not optimized for miRNA detection (C88), which raises questions about the reliability of this finding. The functional speculation (C90) is based on limited prior literature and should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: An orthogonal differential expression analysis using a linear mixed model identified 40 DE genes, with 17 overlapping the primary analysis. This validation approach accounts for shared patient identities across clones.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 describes an important validation analysis. The partial overlap (17/40 genes) between methods suggests some findings are robust to analytical approach, but also indicates sensitivity to statistical modeling choices. The use of a mixed model to account for patient-level effects is methodologically sound, though the modest overlap raises questions about which gene set is more reliable.

results.result: Four DEL clones contained additional CNVs (14q11.1 deletion, 14q11.2 duplication, 7p11.2 deletion). However, there was no significant difference in DE gene expression between clones with and without these additional CNVs, suggesting they are unlikely to account for the reported transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 address potential confounding by additional CNVs. The analysis comparing clones with and without additional CNVs (C92) is appropriate, though the small sample size limits statistical power. The conclusion that additional CNVs are 'unlikely to account' for changes (C93) is reasonable but not definitive—subtle effects could be missed.

results.result: WGCNA identified 123 gene expression modules, with 20 showing significant associations with clinical variables. Fifteen modules correlated with clinical phenotypes, and four modules correlated with Age, Height Z-score, Weight Z-score, and Head Circumference Z-score. GSEA identified 69 gene sets upregulated in high BMI individuals, predominantly in metabolic processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 describe the WGCNA analysis. The identification of modules correlating with clinical traits is interesting, but the analysis is exploratory and correlational. The pink4 module's correlation with multiple traits (C64-C65) is intriguing but requires validation. The predominance of metabolic genes (C63) in BMI-associated modules is consistent with known biology.

results.result: Patient-specific transcriptional abnormalities, in addition to core 16p11.2 transcript deficiency, may interact to generate heterogeneous phenotypes. Gene modules correlating with phenotypic variance involve genes outside the 16p11.2 region and implicate both metabolic and cell-cell signaling pathways. The pink4 module correlates with both BMI and language deficits, suggesting unexpected links between these clinical features.
results.evaluation: Claims C66 and C94-C107 present highly interpretive conclusions from the WGCNA analysis. While the correlations are statistically significant, the causal interpretations are speculative. The suggestion that BMI-associated genes in NPCs reflect 'generalized phenotypes with tissue-specific effects' (C102) is plausible but unproven. The connection between NPC gene expression and language deficits (C103-C104) requires substantial additional validation. These are hypothesis-generating findings rather than established results.

results.result: The hiPSC resource and transcriptomic profiling identified early gene expression alterations in NPCs that precede morphological abnormalities. The data reveal disruptions in gene programs related to nervous system function and cellular metabolism, providing an important resource for studying early neurodevelopmental alterations underlying 16p11.2 CNV phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C74, C112-C113 summarize the overall contributions. The identification of early transcriptional changes (C5) is well-supported by the differential expression data. The characterization of both neural and metabolic disruptions (C6, C74) is supported by the GSEA and WGCNA analyses, though the metabolic findings are more exploratory. The resource value (C112) is clear, though limited by the exclusion of duplication clones.

results.result: Prior work has shown abnormalities in 16p11.2-derived neurons and idiopathic ASD NPCs, and widespread effects on NPC signaling pathways. However, 16p11.2 CNV-related alterations in early neuroepithelial precursors had not been previously examined, representing a gap this study addresses.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 provide context from prior literature and identify the study's contribution. The citations to prior work (C67-C69) are appropriate, and the identification of a gap in the literature (C70) justifies the current study. This establishes the novelty of examining early NPCs rather than more differentiated cell types.
